Claude.notes: Opening chapter uses the Moore's Law → software-development parallel to frame why the course exists — a real problem the concept sections then answer (virtual envs, the .env pattern, temperature 0.0 for classification, unbounded conversation history). Lesson openers cite Karpathy's "English is the hottest programming language" quote, the GPT-3 API history, DeepMind's prompt-as-optimizer paper, and the $14K Reddit chatbot bill — each becomes the exact problem the section resolves. No named fictional protagonist recurs, which is acceptable at Advanced level but leaves character consistency (c4) weak against the strict reading of the criterion.
Claude.topIssue: Labs are AI-assistant conversations, not code executables — a learner cannot literally run the ConversationManager class in-lesson. The lab prompts guide toward the right artifact, but "executability" in the D5 sense means the learner produces working code inside a runnable sandbox, which this module approximates via chat rather than delivers directly.

Gemini.notes: Definitions are mostly precise. Temperature description ("samples the highest-probability token at each step" at 0.0) is correct. Anthropic vs OpenAI system-prompt handling is described accurately (system= top-level param vs role="system" message). The claim "Stack Overflow traffic fell 14% year-over-year in 2024" is a real reported figure but is cited without source; the year framing ("March 2023, OpenAI released GPT-4 with a function-calling API") slightly conflates GPT-4 launch (March 2023) with function-calling GA (June 2023) — a minor precision slip. Tiktoken and exponential-backoff patterns are correctly described.
Gemini.topIssue: Function-calling was announced in June 2023, not at GPT-4's March 2023 launch — the module's opening timeline conflates the two events. This is a small but verifiable factual imprecision in an otherwise strong technical module.

Perplexity.notes: API landscape is largely current for mid-2024 — Copilot subscriber count, Claude/Anthropic system prompt structure, tiktoken workflow. The absence of any 2025-era models (Claude 3.7/4.x, GPT-4.1/GPT-5, Gemini 2.x) is starting to show at the edges: a learner reading this in 2026 will notice the model lineup feels frozen at a moment. Nothing is misleading, but the applied lab of building a "production chatbot" is bound to model families that have moved on.
Perplexity.topIssue: Model references stop at GPT-4o / Claude 3.5 / Gemini 1.5 — the module never mentions the newer generations that dominate developer chatter today. Recommend a refresh pass to add current model IDs and pricing tiers so the ConversationManager cost example stays representative.

Claude.notes: Real-Case openers (three-philosophies month of March 2023, Copilot's FIM prompt engineering, the Lewis-et-al RAG paper, Slack's 300-example fine-tune) each set up a specific engineering question that the concept section then answers — the story-to-concept coupling is tight. Narrative density is calibrated correctly for Advanced (short case → longer concept). Continuity between the four lessons is thematic (model landscape → API → RAG → fine-tune) rather than character-driven.
Claude.topIssue: The four lessons read as four independent essays with no bridge sentences between them; a learner who studies them out of order would notice no continuity thread. Consider adding a one-line callback between lessons ("Now that we've chosen a model, the next question is how to prompt it…") to reinforce narrative arc.

Gemini.notes: LoRA description ("keeps all original model weights frozen and adds pairs of small matrices…only these added matrices are trained") is correct and matches Hu et al. 2021. The RAG cosine-similarity argument (same embedding space required) is technically sound. The Gemini 1.5 Pro "1M+ tokens as of mid-2024" claim is accurate. Mixtral 8x7B as Sparse MoE is correct. One place to tighten: the module implies the March 2023 releases (GPT-4 report, PaLM 2 paper, LLaMA weights) all happened in "a single month" — LLaMA weights leaked in early March, GPT-4 launched March 14, PaLM 2 was announced at I/O in May, so "a single month" is slightly loose.
Gemini.topIssue: PaLM 2 was announced at Google I/O in May 2023, not "the same week" as the GPT-4 technical report — the "three philosophies in a single month" framing collapses a two-month window. Tighten the timeline claim.

Perplexity.notes: Model-landscape framing is anchored to "2024 landscape" and this dating is now visible — the quiz asks about the "largest publicly documented context window as of mid-2024," which reads as a historical question in 2026. The RAG paper citation (Lewis et al., FAIR, 2020) and Slack fine-tune anecdote hold up. The Model Selection Advisor lab still functions today, but the recommendations it will pattern-match against are from a moment where Claude 3.5 was the frontier and o1/GPT-5-class reasoning models did not exist.
Perplexity.topIssue: The "2024 landscape" quiz question and the module's pricing/context references are now dated — a learner in 2026 will have to mentally re-baseline against current model tiers, and the lab's Model Selection Advisor will reason from an out-of-date map of the market.

Claude.notes: BloombergGPT vs Alpaca/Vicuna as the opening framing is a strong problem-creator — the story ("tens of millions vs under $600") makes the exact question the lesson answers vivid. Orca-2 as a "data quality over volume" case study lands the insight naturally. Mistral-7B's "learning rates 10-100× too high for LoRA" is a specific, memorable insight. Med-PaLM 2's dual eval story frames the evaluation lesson with real stakes.
Claude.topIssue: The narrative sometimes sprints past the insight — Lesson 1's "Pre-training vs Fine-tuning" concept section jumps into hyperparameter territory that arguably belongs in Lesson 3. Consider trimming Lesson 1's scope so it lands one insight (what fine-tuning is) before the mechanics arrive.

Gemini.notes: LoRA rank-r description (matrix shapes d×r and r×d, higher r = more capacity) is accurate. SFT vs DPO framing is correct at this level of depth. The "Stanford Alpaca 52K instructions ~$600" figure is real (Alpaca used 52K self-instruct examples, Stanford quoted ~$500-600 in fine-tuning cost). The Orca claim ("13B model outperformed larger models on reasoning benchmarks") is faithful to the paper but understates the caveat that this was against non-reasoning-tuned baselines. Med-PaLM 2 dual-eval story is accurate.
Gemini.topIssue: The Orca comparison is real but under-caveated — Orca outperformed same-size baselines, not systematically larger frontier models on all tasks. The quiz language "outperformed larger models" would benefit from "outperformed comparably-sized models and some larger baselines on specific reasoning tasks."

Perplexity.notes: Fine-tuning fundamentals are stable knowledge and age well. However, the tooling references (OpenAI fine-tune API, Mistral 7B, LoRA rank defaults) are anchored to 2023-2024; the field has since shifted toward preference-optimization stacks (DPO/ORPO/KTO) and higher-quality open-model bases (Llama 3.1/3.3, Qwen 2.5/3, Mistral Nemo). The module's "when to fine-tune" advice still lands, but a learner shopping for base models today will not find the current defaults reflected.
Perplexity.topIssue: DPO is mentioned but not developed; ORPO/KTO/SimPO — now common alternatives to SFT+DPO — are absent. The base-model recommendations should be refreshed to reflect current open-model families a learner would actually select in 2026.

Claude.notes: Strongest module for narrative-concept coupling. Databricks DBRX benchmark (31% → 78% with retrieval) creates the retrieval-vs-parametric-memory problem the entire lesson answers. Klarna's "11 minutes → 2 minutes" is a concrete win-condition. Notion's query-rewriting +22% and Microsoft GraphRAG's 72% global-reasoning win are precise, well-attributed anchor cases. The module escalates cleanly: fundamentals → vector stores → advanced retrieval → production/GraphRAG. Labs match production scale (50K contracts, 10M-vector migration, 68%→85% target, hedge-fund observability).
Claude.topIssue: The four lessons rely on real-company cases as the recurring "character" — this works but means a learner never meets a person navigating the problem, only a company. A single running case study (e.g. "you're the ML engineer at MidsizeCo, and every lesson you're at a new stage") would tighten narrative continuity.

Gemini.notes: HyDE definition is precise ("LLM generates a hypothetical ideal answer, then that answer is embedded and used as the retrieval query"). GraphRAG description matches the Microsoft Research paper (community-level sensemaking, extracted entity relationships). The embedding-space consistency point is technically correct and non-negotiable. Chunking strategies, HNSW tuning, and quantization are described at correct depth. The "1.2M QPS on 10M-vector SIFT dataset" claim tracks published Qdrant benchmarks but ANN-Benchmarks specifically is more nuanced — Qdrant leads on some subsets, not all.
Gemini.topIssue: The Qdrant "1.2M queries per second" figure needs the benchmark caveat: it is a specific dataset (SIFT), specific recall target (95%@1), single-node — the module should note this is a headline number, not a general claim. Otherwise learners will over-index on Qdrant as universally fastest.

Perplexity.notes: The most current-feeling module in the course — Microsoft GraphRAG (July 2024) and Klarna (Feb 2024) are anchor references and they still hold. Vector-store landscape (Pinecone / Qdrant / Weaviate / Chroma / pgvector) is roughly current for 2026, though it now competes with LanceDB, Turbopuffer, and native Postgres extensions that gained traction post-2024. Reranker discussion pairs well with the current Cohere Rerank v3 / bge-reranker line. Production-observability guidance (langsmith / phoenix / traceloop equivalents) is described as concepts rather than tools, which ages well.
Perplexity.topIssue: Vector-store market has fragmented since — LanceDB, Turbopuffer, and hosted pgvector variants deserve mention as viable alternatives for the "10K→10M scaling" lab, whose recommendations would otherwise skew toward the 2024 shortlist.

Claude.notes: Google Bard's James Webb hallucination opening ($100B market-cap drop) is one of the most story-forward openings in the course — the failure is concrete, dated, memorable, and the concept ("no metric in their release pipeline was measuring factual grounding") is the exact insight the lesson delivers. BIG-bench contamination, Chatbot Arena sycophancy bias, and GitHub Copilot's 40% insecure-code finding each work the same way. Cognitive framing ("How do I know when to ship?") is Advanced-appropriate.
Claude.topIssue: Lesson 4's "silent security regression" story (Copilot 40%) sits in the Evaluation module but arguably belongs to the Monitoring module too — some content overlaps M6. Consider a cross-reference line so learners know the fuller monitoring story arrives in Module 6.

Gemini.notes: Precision/recall/accuracy trade-off framing (cancer-screening example, spam filter with 98%/15%) is textbook-correct and pedagogically effective. LLM-as-judge failure modes (verbosity bias, position bias, self-preference) are all real and correctly named. The BLEU-score critique reflects the current research consensus that BLEU is a poor proxy for generation quality. One caveat: the Chatbot Arena "500,000+ human preference votes" is under-cited — LMSYS has published multi-million vote totals; the module's number is a snapshot from a specific 2023 checkpoint and should be dated.
Gemini.topIssue: The "500K+ Chatbot Arena votes" figure is a stale snapshot — LMSYS has since crossed millions of votes across many model generations. State the snapshot date or refresh the number.

Perplexity.notes: Evaluation methodology (CheckList, capability tests, LLM-as-judge, shadow deployment) is stable material and ages well. The Bard James Webb incident is a permanent reference. RAGAS / DeepEval / Phoenix are absent but the module wisely stays framework-agnostic. What is now missing is the post-2024 discussion of long-context eval (needle-in-haystack limits, RULER benchmark), reasoning-model evaluation (o1-style/thinking-model traces), and agentic-task evaluation frameworks — all of which have become mainstream since this content was written.
Perplexity.topIssue: No coverage of reasoning-model evaluation (chain-of-thought trace scoring, thinking-token accounting) or agentic-task benchmarks (SWE-bench, tau-bench) — both are now core evaluation concerns a 2026 practitioner would expect to see.

Claude.notes: ChatGPT's Nov-2022 capacity crisis opens the module with a real infra-scale problem; Meta's "silent model rot" (output-distribution monitoring) is a durable insight; Google's tiered eval (Tier 1 golden set → Tier 2 LLM-as-judge → Tier 3 human) gives learners a concrete architecture to imitate; Brex's tiered routing story lands the cost lesson. Continuous, clinical-note-summarisation labs form a single running case, which is the strongest continuity thread in the course.
Claude.topIssue: The recurring "clinical note summarisation tool" across labs is a nice throughline but the concept sections never reference it — merge them so the concept sections walk through the same scenario the labs use.

Gemini.notes: PagedAttention description ("OS-style virtual memory paging to the KV cache, eliminating fragmentation") is faithful to the vLLM paper. Continuous batching definition is precise. Quantization (Int8/4-bit AWQ/GPTQ implied) is described at appropriate depth. Semantic caching threshold (cosine > 0.95-0.97) is a reasonable operational default. Meta "silent model rot" is a real Meta engineering-blog concept and correctly named. The "7B in BFloat16 requires ~14GB VRAM" arithmetic (7B × 2 bytes/param) is correct.
Gemini.topIssue: The BFloat16 sizing quiz omits KV-cache VRAM which dominates at long context — a learner will size a 7B system to 14GB and be surprised when concurrent 32K-context requests OOM. Add KV-cache sizing to the concept section.

Perplexity.notes: vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM are still the dominant serving stacks in 2026, so the module's framework choices remain current. Grafana + Prometheus + trace-observability guidance ages well. What is missing: SGLang and vLLM v1 (post-2024 rewrite) are now standard; speculative decoding is now table-stakes for latency-sensitive workloads; disaggregated prefill/decode serving (deepseek-vllm, NVIDIA Dynamo) has become the recommended architecture for large-scale deployments. The Brex tiered-routing pattern is now often replaced with LLM routers (Martian, Not-Diamond, Portkey).
Perplexity.topIssue: Speculative decoding, disaggregated prefill/decode serving, and LLM-router products (which reshaped this space in 2024-2025) are absent — a learner who ships from this module will design an architecture one generation behind current best practice.

Claude.notes: Zillow Offers ($881M loss, Nov 2021), Netflix's three-generation architecture arc, Amazon's 2017 recruiting-tool bias, and COVID-19 demand-forecasting drift are four of the most-cited system-design failure cases in the industry — each creates the exact problem the corresponding lesson answers. Cognitive framing sits squarely at Advanced ("what does the requirement need to say before I can build?"). The Requirements Elicitation Workshop lab (turn "reduce delivery failures" into a testable spec) is one of the best-designed labs in the course.
Claude.topIssue: The module is heavy on ML-system cases and light on LLM-specific system-design pitfalls (prompt drift, tool-call reliability, context-window budgeting, agent step-limits). A future revision could add at least one LLM-native failure case alongside the classical ML ones.

Gemini.notes: Zillow Offers root-cause attribution ("failing to define error tolerances and operational envelope") matches the post-mortem consensus. Amazon 2017 recruiting-tool bias attribution to feature-engineering-encoded historical bias is correct. Netflix's batch → online → two-tower generational arc is faithful to their engineering blog. COVID-19 concept-drift framing ("no drift detection was present") is technically precise. Data-pipeline case (credit scoring with target leakage from "days since last payment computed at prediction time") is a textbook example of train/serve skew and correctly diagnosed.
Gemini.topIssue: The credit-scoring lab implicitly assumes learners will spot both target leakage AND unsaved-scaler skew — the setup packs two subtle bugs into one scenario. Consider splitting into two labs so each bug lands cleanly.

Perplexity.notes: System-design principles (requirements before architecture, monitoring layers, graceful degradation) are timeless and age well. The Zillow / Netflix / Amazon / COVID case studies are permanent references. What is now missing from a 2026 vantage point: agent-system design (tool-use loops, step budgets, error recovery), MCP-server-style tool integration, and multi-agent orchestration patterns are the architectural questions dominating current practice. The module's architecture-pattern catalog is complete for classical ML+LLM systems but silent on agentic ones.
Perplexity.topIssue: No coverage of agentic-system design (tool-loop step budgets, plan-execute-critique patterns, agent error recovery) — this is now a major slice of what "AI system design" means in 2026 and its absence dates the module.

Claude.notes: Best-structured module in the course. Semantic Scholar's one-sentence success statement, Klarna's "boring architecture" (700 FTE workload with a stateless FastAPI + Weaviate + Claude stack), Harvey AI's TypeScript-schema prompt engineering (94% JSON-parse-failure reduction), and Intercom Fin's shadow deployment (2.3% hallucination rate on pricing) are four of the best-attributed real-world case studies I have seen in an AI course. The four labs (Scope → Architecture → Prompt → Capstone Review) build on each other explicitly — the capstone integration review references artifacts from all three prior labs, which is the strongest continuity thread in the entire course. Cognitive framing (produce a deployable spec) is right at the top of Bloom's taxonomy for Advanced.
Claude.topIssue: The Capstone Integration Review lab is graded by an AI reviewer — a human sign-off gate (peer review, mentor review) at the end would strengthen the "deployable" claim, since real deployment reviews are inter-human events.

Gemini.notes: Klarna's Feb-2024 "700 FTE agent workload" is a publicly documented figure. Harvey AI's TypeScript-schema technique is a real published pattern (contract-first prompting). Intercom Fin's shadow-deployment methodology is faithful to their published engineering blog. Semantic Scholar/Allen Institute recommendation-engine framing is accurate. Scope-template ("For [user], when [trigger], the system will [output] so that [outcome], with error rate [threshold]") is a solid derivative of the standard user-story format extended with an ML-specific success metric.
Gemini.topIssue: The Klarna "700 FTE" claim is real but Klarna's later reporting acknowledged mixed results and partial re-humanisation of the workflow — the module should note this update rather than freeze the story at the peak moment.

Perplexity.notes: Capstone framing (scope → architecture → prompt → deploy) is a durable pattern that transcends any specific model generation. Case studies (Klarna, Harvey AI, Intercom Fin) are from 2023-2024 and their pattern lessons still hold. What is now dated: prompt-architecture guidance leans on "system-prompt-as-TypeScript-type" which has been partly superseded by structured-outputs / JSON-mode / native tool-schemas at the API layer; the "contract prompt" pattern still works but is no longer state-of-the-art. Klarna's AI-support outcome should also be updated with 2025 reporting on the partial roll-back.
Perplexity.topIssue: Structured-outputs and native JSON-mode APIs (available across all frontier providers by mid-2024) reduce the need for TypeScript-in-prompt patterns — the module should present this as one option, not the leading one.
